subject: chemistry-2
question: A blood sample's pH is reported as 7.2, compared with a previous value of 7.4 in the same person. Which interpretation of this change is most accurate?

options.text: Hydronium ion concentration rose by about 0.2 mol/L

explanation:
A fall in pH always corresponds to a rise in hydronium concentration, and the magnitude of that rise is 10 raised to the pH difference: 10^(7.4 - 7.2) = 10^0.2, which is about 1.58. So a 0.2-unit drop represents roughly a 58 percent increase in [H3O+]. Option B would require a 2-unit fall, option C reverses the direction of the relationship, and option D misreads a pH difference as a concentration difference in mol/L.

ELI-10: Two features of pH have to be applied together here: it runs in reverse, so a lower number means more hydronium, and it is logarithmic, so even a fractional change multiplies the concentration. Raising 10 to the 0.2 power gives about 1.6, meaning roughly 60 percent more hydronium than before. In absolute terms the shift is from about 4 × 10^-8 to about 6 × 10^-8 mol/L, tiny numbers whose ratio is what matters physiologically.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)
